paragraphs.text: How can two strangers agree on a secret key when anyone can read their messages?
They never send the key. Each person keeps a private number...
This method is the Diffie–Hellman key exchange. A version of it starts most HTTPS connections.
Alice and Bob want to encrypt their messages...
A first idea fails. Alice picks the key, 6, and sends 5^6 mod 23 = 8...

paragraphs.text: "mod 23" means "the remainder after division by 23"...
Alice and Bob agree in public on two numbers: a prime modulus p = 23 and a base g = 5.

paragraphs.text: Each picks a private number at random...
Each sends a public number: g raised to their private number, mod p...
Each raises the other's public number to their own private number, mod p...
The result, s = 2, is the shared secret...
Alice computed (5^15)^6, and Bob computed (5^6)^15...

Multiplying fails: 8 × 19 mod 23 = 152 mod 23 = 14...

paragraphs.text: Each choice blocks a simpler way for Eve to find a private number.
Without mod, A = 5^6 = 15625. Eve takes the logarithm base 5...
With multiplication instead of a power, A = 5 × 6 mod 23 = 7...
With powers mod p, the results jump around...
So g^x mod p is a one-way operation... the discrete logarithm.

paragraphs.text: No one has proven that the discrete logarithm is hard...
The exchange stops a reader. It does not stop Mallory...
Alice computes 10^6 mod 23 = 6... Bob computes 10^15 mod 23 = 5...
Alice shares 6 with Mallory, and Bob shares 5 with Mallory...
The two strangers never send the key...
Authentication... Elliptic-curve... hash function... AES... Quantum computers

question.text: How can two parties who share only a public channel, one that an eavesdropper can read, end up with the same secret key?
question.known_at: Title (line 1), with the setting made concrete at line 9
question.result_stated: Yes, in words at line 3: "They never send the key. Each person keeps a private number and sends a public number computed from it... no known fast method gets the private numbers back from them."

reply.motive: Reason to care: "A version of it starts most HTTPS connections." (line 5). Reason for the approach: "A first idea fails... If Eve cannot get 6 back from 8, Bob cannot either. So each side needs its own private number." (line 12). Also "Each choice blocks a simpler way for Eve to find a private number." (line 43), followed by the three bullets.
reply.close: Yes. Line 75 reads: "Each sends g raised to a private number, mod p. Each raises the other's public number to their own private number, and both get g^(ab) mod p. Eve sees only g^a and g^b mod p. To get further, Eve must find a or b, and no fast method is known for a large p."
reply.recap: Each side sends 5 raised to a secret power, remainder 23. Each then raises the other's number to its own secret power, so both reach 5^(ab). Eve can't do this because getting the exponent back out of the remainder is believed to be infeasibly slow.
reply.strongest: 'Why powers, and why mod' (lines 43-52). It rules out plain powers (logarithm) and multiplication (an inverse via Euclid) with concrete numbers, then shows the scrambled table of 5^x mod 23.
reply.weakest: Line 12. It uses 'mod' four lines before defining it, and 'one half of a calculation... the other side finishes it' stays abstract until the steps arrive.
suggestions: Define 'mod' before line 12, or move the 'first idea fails' paragraph to after the definition.
Add a short clause saying why p is prime, for example so that the powers of g can cover many values.
Say in a few words that k in (x + 23k) is any whole number.
